broad.question: For steels used in chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain their resistance to corrosion? Specify a controlled study capable of revealing the governing cause, predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, supporting evidence from prior findings, and a result that would falsify it.

final_hypothesis.label: C1

source_paper.title: Effect of Silicon on Dynamic/Static Corrosion Resistance of T91 in Lead-Bismuth Eutectic at 550 °C.

final_hypothesis.builds_on: The paper shows that increased Si content promotes the formation of a stable, protective oxide film in T91 steel via selective oxidation (PMC9028533::web::026::4_discussion). This hypothesis extends that mechanism by controlling the oxygen chemical potential during post-processing to further tailor the oxide layer composition.
final_hypothesis.what_is_new: This approach introduces a deliberate post-treatment step under controlled oxygen conditions (not used in the paper) to pre-form an optimized duplex oxide film, decoupling the oxidation kinetics from in-service uncontrolled oxidation.

hypothesis.hypothesis: A controlled post-processing annealing in a slightly oxidizing atmosphere will promote the selective formation of a thin, duplex oxide film in Si-enhanced T91 steel, where the inner layer is enriched in Cr and Si and the outer layer is limited in Fe-oxide growth, thereby slowing overall corrosion in aggressive environments.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: T91 steel with moderate Si content (≈1.3 wt.%) produced via conventional melting, forging, normalizing at 1050 °C, and tempering at 770 °C.
hypothesis.intervention: Introduce an annealing step immediately after tempering under a controlled low oxygen partial pressure (e.g., using a gas mixture with a known, moderate oxygen concentration) at a temperature near service conditions (500–550 °C) for a short duration.
hypothesis.conditions: Expose the treated samples to aggressive high-temperature environments (550 °C) relevant to chemical-processing or nuclear-power applications, with oxygen potentials comparable to those controlled during the annealing step. Control experiments would use samples processed under standard inert or vacuum atmospheres.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A pre-formed, coherent duplex oxide scale consisting of an inner Cr/Si-rich layer and a limited outer Fe-rich oxide layer.
hypothesis.mechanism: The modest oxygen potential during the additional annealing favors the preferential oxidation of Cr and Si (both having highly negative ΔGθ for oxidation, as indicated by the reaction energy for Si oxidation ~−777.89 kJ/mol from PMC9028533::web::026::4_discussion) while suppressing rapid Fe oxidation. This pre-formed oxide scale then acts as an effective diffusion barrier against further oxygen ingress and Fe outward migration during service.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to baseline samples, the treated samples will develop a significantly thinner, more uniform duplex oxide film (reducing the parabolic rate constant, kp, e.g., by 20–30% if supported by kinetic comparisons) and exhibit lower weight loss or corrosion rate upon exposure.
hypothesis.baseline: Standard T91 steel with ≈1.3 wt.% Si processed without the controlled oxygen annealing step, which in service forms thicker, less controlled multi-layered oxide films.
hypothesis.boundary: The beneficial effect is expected at service temperatures between 500 and 550 °C under oxidizing environments with moderate oxygen potentials. Under extremely reducing or excessively oxidizing conditions, the selective oxidation kinetics might not yield the desired duplex structure.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The exact oxygen partial pressure and duration needed to achieve the optimal balance between selective Cr/Si oxidation and minimal Fe oxidation must be empirically determined; quantitative improvements in kp are uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of T91 steel samples with ~1.3 wt.% Si: one set undergoes the additional annealing in a controlled low oxygen atmosphere (at 550 °C for a predetermined short duration) and the other set is processed by the standard inert atmosphere route. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature corrosion testing conditions (550 °C in a simulated aggressive environment).
measurements: Cross-sectional SEM/EPMA to evaluate oxide layer thickness and composition
Weight loss measurements and parabolic rate constant (kp) determination
Surface adhesion and continuity of oxide layers (optical/SEM imaging)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the treated samples do not display a significantly thinner, more continuous duplex oxide (with demonstrably lower kp and weight loss) compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C3

source_paper.title: Effect of Silicon on Dynamic/Static Corrosion Resistance of T91 in Lead-Bismuth Eutectic at 550 °C.

top3.builds_on: The paper demonstrates that Si enhances the formation of protective oxide layers in T91 steel (PMC9028533::web::026::4_discussion). This hypothesis leverages that by adding a reactive element known to improve oxide adhesion, thereby potentially further enhancing the integrity and protective performance of the duplex oxide scale.
top3.what_is_new: It introduces the concept of reactive element microalloying (using Y) to stabilize the protective oxide film in Si-enhanced T91 steel—a strategy not explored in the original paper, representing a novel alloy design modification for improved corrosion resistance.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Addition of trace reactive elements such as yttrium (Y) to Si-enhanced T91 steel will promote grain-boundary segregation in the oxide scale, improving its adhesion and continuity and thus enhancing corrosion resistance under harsh chemical-processing and nuclear-power conditions.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: T91 steel with a moderate Si content (≈1.3 wt.%) produced by conventional melting, forging, normalizing, and tempering, resulting in a tempered martensitic microstructure with typical carbide distributions.
hypothesis.intervention: Incorporate a small, controlled addition of Y (e.g., 0.03–0.1 wt.%) during alloy production so that during subsequent high-temperature exposure, Y segregates to grain boundaries and interfaces within the forming oxide scale.
hypothesis.conditions: Expose the Y-doped and conventional (no Y addition) T91 steels to high-temperature corrosive conditions at around 550 °C, in environments typical for chemical-processing and nuclear-power applications (static and dynamic LBE or comparable media).
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Enhanced grain boundary segregation of Y, which aids in stabilizing and binding the duplex oxide scale (notably the Si-rich and Cr-rich layers), reducing the likelihood of spallation or crack formation.
hypothesis.mechanism: Reactive elements like Y are known to improve oxide scale adhesion (the reactive element effect) by segregating to the oxide-metal interface and grain boundaries. In the context of Si-enhanced T91 steel, trace Y is expected to accumulate preferentially at locations where the Cr/Si oxides nucleate, thereby reducing interfacial energy and enhancing scale cohesiveness. This results in a more coherent and continuous protective barrier that impedes both oxygen ingress and Fe outward diffusion.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Compared to baseline T91 steel, the Y-doped material will manifest a more uniform, continuous, and thinner duplex oxide layer with improved adhesion, translating into a measurable reduction in the corrosion rate (e.g., a lower kp constant and weight loss) upon prolonged exposure at 550 °C.
hypothesis.baseline: T91 steel with ~1.3 wt.% Si manufactured without Y additions, which develops an oxide scale that may have discontinuities or poor adhesion due to the absence of reactive element effects.
hypothesis.boundary: The beneficial effect of Y is anticipated under high-temperature oxidizing conditions (around 550 °C) where the reactive element effect is operative; performance in highly reducing atmospheres or at temperatures far from the processing regime may not be significantly improved.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While the reactive element effect has been demonstrated in various high-temperature alloys (e.g., nickel-based systems), its quantitative impact in ferritic–martensitic steels like T91 with moderate Si content requires further validation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of T91 steel samples with ~1.3 wt.% Si: one set with a trace addition of Y (e.g., 0.05 wt.%) and a control set without Y. Subject both sets to identical high-temperature corrosion tests at 550 °C in a simulated aggressive environment. Use advanced microscopy and surface analysis to examine oxide scale continuity and adhesion.
measurements: Oxide scale morphology and thickness (via cross-sectional SEM/TEM)
Elemental mapping to detect Y segregation at the oxide-metal interface (via EPMA or EDS)
Corrosion rate determination through weight loss and/or electrochemical tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If Y-doped samples do not exhibit significantly improved oxide scale adhesion (i.e., comparable or worse oxide film continuity, thickness, or corrosion rates) relative to the control, then the hypothesis is falsified.

source_paper.title: Design for improving corrosion resistance of duplex stainless steels by wrapping inclusions with niobium armour.

top3.builds_on: the paper’s finding that hot working and subsequent aging promote the formation of a Z‐phase that wraps inclusions, by further exploiting strain-induced nucleation mechanisms
top3.what_is_new: It proposes a deliberate, controlled thermo‐mechanical processing route (warm deformation plus aging) to actively enhance the nucleation, distribution, and alignment of the protective Nb-rich Z‐phase around inclusions, thereby further mitigating localized corrosion risks.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Controlled Thermo‐Mechanical Processing to Promote Strain‐Induced Nucleation and Alignment of Protective Z‐Phase Shells around Inclusions in Duplex Stainless Steels
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Duplex stainless steel (e.g., S32205) fabricated by conventional routes, containing randomly distributed nonmetallic inclusions (such as MgAl2O4 and MnS) and a Nb-induced Z‐phase forming during standard hot working and heat treatment.
hypothesis.intervention: Implement a carefully controlled thermo‐mechanical processing schedule that includes a warm deformation step (e.g., controlled rolling or forging at an intermediate temperature around 700 °C) immediately prior to a tailored aging treatment. This is designed to introduce advantageous defect structures (dislocations) that act as additional heterogeneous nucleation sites for the Nb‐rich Z‐phase.
hypothesis.conditions: Prepare two sets of specimens: one processed with the conventional hot working/heat treatment route, and another subjected to the additional controlled warm deformation and subsequent aging treatment. Test both sets in simulated chemical-processing environments (e.g., high chloride solutions at ~72 °C) and under conditions representative of nuclear power plant coolants.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Enhanced and more uniformly distributed nucleation of Nb‐rich Z‐phase precipitates that wrap inclusions, promoted by deformation-induced dislocations and strain fields.
hypothesis.mechanism: The strain introduced during the warm deformation step generates a high density of dislocations, which serve as preferential nucleation sites for Nb-rich Z‐phase precipitates during the following aging treatment. This results in a more continuous and well-aligned protective shell around nonmetallic inclusions. By effectively covering the inclusion/matrix interfaces, the approach minimizes local galvanic differences and corrosive attack. This strategy extends the paper’s observation that hot working promotes Z-phase formation by deliberately engineering the deformation conditions.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Specimens processed with the controlled thermo‐mechanical route should exhibit a higher percentage of inclusions encapsulated by a continuous and well-aligned Z‐phase shell, as evidenced by TEM/EDS analysis. Correspondingly, electrochemical tests (potentiodynamic polarization) will show a higher pitting potential and lower corrosion current densities, with reduced pit density and depth compared to the conventionally processed baseline.
hypothesis.baseline: Duplex stainless steels processed using the standard hot working and heat treatment protocols without the additional controlled warm deformation and aging step.
hypothesis.boundary: The effectiveness of the strain-induced nucleation mechanism is expected to be notable in duplex stainless steels where the initial inclusion size and distribution allow for enhanced nucleation without deleteriously affecting the bulk mechanical properties. The approach is applicable when the processing route permits precise control over deformation parameters.
hypothesis.uncertainty: It is uncertain whether the induced deformation might inadvertently introduce additional defects that compromise overall material integrity, and the optimal deformation strain and temperature require thorough parameter optimization.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two groups of S32205 duplex stainless steel samples: one using the conventional processing route and one with the additional controlled warm deformation (at ~700 °C, with optimized strain) followed by aging. Characterize the microstructure using TEM and electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) to quantify the extent and alignment of Z-phase shells around inclusions. Perform potentiodynamic polarization tests and immersion corrosion experiments to compare corrosion performance.
measurements: Fraction and continuity of inclusions wrapped by Z-phase (via TEM/EBSD)
Quantitative corrosion parameters (pitting potential, corrosion current density, pit depth/density)
Assessment of dislocation density and strain fields near inclusion interfaces
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the additional thermo‐mechanical processing does not result in a statistically significant increase in both the extent of Z-phase wrapping and the associated improvements in corrosion performance compared to the baseline, then the hypothesis is falsified.

final_hypothesis.label: C6

source_paper.title: The Synergistic Inhibitions of Tungstate and Molybdate Anions on Pitting Corrosion Initiation for Q235 Carbon Steel in Chloride Solution.

final_hypothesis.builds_on: The paper’s observation that WO42− and MoO42− can modify the passive film composition to yield films with lower defect density and higher resistance to chloride attack.
final_hypothesis.what_is_new: This hypothesis innovates by shifting the incorporation of tungsten and molybdate anions to a pre-treatment step via controlled electrochemical polarization, thereby pre-forming a protective passive film before exposure to corrosive environments.

hypothesis.hypothesis: An electrochemical polarization pre-treatment of Q235 steel in an electrolyte containing low concentrations of tungstate and molybdate anions can induce the formation of an enriched, defect-scarce passive film that suppresses pitting corrosion in aggressive chloride environments.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Pre-exposure Q235 steel prepared in the standard abraded (1000-grit) state.
hypothesis.intervention: Subject the steel to a controlled anodic polarization hold in an aqueous electrolyte containing low-level concentrations of Na2WO4 and Na2MoO4 (below concentrations that could cause PC initiation in chloride), prior to exposure to the harsh environment.
hypothesis.conditions: Perform the pre-treatment at room temperature; then test corrosion behavior in chloride-containing solutions at both room temperature and elevated temperature (e.g., 60 °C).
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A nascent passive film enriched with tungsten and molybdenum compounds (similar to Fe2(WO4)3 and Fe2(MoO4)3) that has fewer defects as indicated by lower donor density (ND) in Mott–Schottky plots.
hypothesis.mechanism: Controlled anodic polarization in the presence of WO42− and MoO42− facilitates the formation of a proto-passive film that incorporates these anions. This film undergoes a structural rearrangement yielding a denser, more homogeneous oxide that resists aggressive chloride ion penetration. The mechanism relates to improved repair of film defects via the incorporation of Mo and W, as seen in the paper’s synergistic inhibition analysis.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Polarized pre-treated samples will show an elevated pitting potential and reduced pitting site density relative to untreated samples. EIS and Mott–Schottky analyses will indicate increased outer film resistance and reduced defect density.
hypothesis.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel with no electrochemical pre-conditioning, exhibiting standard passive film formation when first exposed to chloride environments.
hypothesis.boundary: The method is applicable when the polarization conditions are carefully controlled to avoid over-oxidation or inducing early pitting; its effectiveness might be sensitive to the precise electrolyte composition and pre-treatment duration.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Exact polarization parameters and the optimum WO42−/MoO42− concentration for film enrichment are uncertain and must be determined experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Q235 steel specimens: one group receives the electrochemical pre-treatment (anodic polarization in a WO42−/MoO42− containing electrolyte) and the other is left untreated. Expose both groups to chloride-rich solutions at controlled room and elevated temperatures. Evaluate corrosion behavior using potentiodynamic polarization, EIS, and Mott–Schottky analysis, and examine the passive film composition via XPS.
measurements: Shift in pitting potential (Ep)
Film resistance and capacitance from EIS
Defect density (donor density) from Mott–Schottky plots
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If pre-treated samples do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in pitting potential, film resistance, or a reduction in defect density compared to the untreated control, the hypothesis is falsified.

source_paper.title: Effects of Cold Rolling on the Microstructure and Corrosion Resistance of the Double-Glow Plasma Ni-Cr Alloying Layer on Q235 Steel.

top3.builds_on: The mechanism builds on established principles of aluminizing treatments in high-temperature alloys and the protective nature of alumina layers as described in the background for oxide-forming strategies.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis applies a controlled, localized aluminum diffusion process to plain Q235 steel, aiming to create an in situ protective alumina barrier—a method distinct from plasma alloying—to test direct improvements in corrosion resistance under both room temperature and elevated temperature conditions.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Incorporating a minimal, surface-localized aluminum enrichment via a low-temperature aluminizing diffusion step can form a transient subscale of alumina that mitigates corrosion degradation by acting as a stable barrier against oxidation and chloride attack at both room and elevated temperatures.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Untreated Q235 steel with its native surface oxide, which is not optimized for high temperature or aggressive media resistance.
hypothesis.intervention: Perform a brief, low-temperature aluminizing treatment (e.g., pack cementation or low-energy ion implantation of Al) to achieve a shallow diffusion of aluminum into the surface.
hypothesis.conditions: Expose both the aluminized and the pristine Q235 steel specimens to a 5% H2SO4 and 3.5% NaCl environment at ambient temperature and at an elevated temperature (e.g., 80–100 °C) to simulate harsh conditions.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Formation of a thin, adherent Al-oxide (alumina) interlayer at the steel surface, which is thermodynamically more stable than iron oxides and has a lower diffusivity for oxygen and aggressive species.
hypothesis.mechanism: Aluminum is more reactive with oxygen than iron, and even in trace amounts can form a dense, continuous alumina layer. This layer acts as a robust physical and chemical barrier, significantly slowing further oxidation and metal dissolution, similar to the protection observed in alumina-forming stainless steels.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Aluminized specimens are expected to show a higher corrosion potential and a lower corrosion current density relative to untreated Q235 steel, with evidence of a thin alumina layer upon surface analysis.
hypothesis.baseline: The untreated Q235 steel surface with its native, non-optimized oxide, which is comparatively less protective in harsh environments.
hypothesis.boundary: The diffusion process must be calibrated to avoid excessive aluminum uptake that could affect bulk mechanical properties. The protective effect relies on retaining a very thin alumina layer; any failure in forming or maintaining this layer would negate the benefits.
hypothesis.uncertainty: While alumina’s protective properties are well established in stainless steels, the quantitative corrosion resistance improvement on low-alloy Q235 steel with minimal aluminum addition is not precisely predictable.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel specimens: one set treated by the low-temperature aluminizing process and one set remaining untreated. Subject both sets to corrosion testing in 5% H2SO4 and 3.5% NaCl environments at room temperature and at elevated temperatures (80–100 °C). Analyze the surfaces using XPS or SEM-EDS to confirm the presence of an alumina layer, and perform potentiodynamic polarization tests.
measurements: Corrosion potential
Corrosion current density
Surface composition and oxide phase identification
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the aluminized specimens do not form a consistent alumina layer or do not demonstrate a statistically significant improvement in corrosion resistance relative to the untreated specimens, the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C3

source_paper.title: Electrochemical corrosion behaviour of four low-carbon steels in saline soil.

top3.builds_on: The finding from PMC9302071 that Q235 corrosion is mass transfer controlled, suggesting that altering the diffusion barrier (i.e., a pre-formed oxide film) could modulate the corrosion process.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis proposes a deliberate surface pre-passivation step for Q235 steel prior to exposure in saline soil, which the paper did not explore; it links controlled anodic oxidation with suppression of mass transfer dominated corrosion.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Pre-passivation of Q235 steel by controlled anodic oxidation will form a thin, uniform, and adherent oxide layer that suppresses oxygen diffusion and the associated mass-transfer limited corrosion process in saline environments.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: As-received, mechanically polished Q235 steel with a mill-finished surface exhibiting inherent heterogeneities.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a controlled anodic oxidation treatment (e.g., in a dilute alkaline electrolyte at controlled potentials) to pre-form a compact oxide film on the Q235 surface.
hypothesis.conditions: Exposure tests in natural saline soil (1.1% salt content) at room temperature (20 °C) and at an elevated temperature regime (e.g., 50 °C) to assess temperature effects on the preformed film stability.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A thin, dense iron oxide film with decreased porosity and fewer micro-defects.
hypothesis.mechanism: The pre-formed compact oxide layer inhibits the ingress of corrosive species (oxygen and Cl⁻ ions), thereby mitigating the mass transfer of reactants to the steel surface. Since the paper indicates that Q235 corrosion is controlled by mass transfer (PMC9302071::web::000, PMC9302071::web::015), modifying the diffusion layer should delay the onset and propagation of corrosion.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: The anodized Q235 samples will exhibit a slower increase in corrosion current/density, a higher charge transfer resistance over time (via EIS), and reduced weight loss compared to untreated Q235. The improvement is expected to be moderate (directionally significant but roughly on the order of a 20–40% reduction in corrosion rate), though precise values are uncertain.
hypothesis.baseline: Untreated Q235 steel tested under identical saline soil conditions.
hypothesis.boundary: The effect is likely dependent on the quality and stability of the oxide film; excessively thick or non-adherent films may lead to spallation under thermal cycling.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Exact quantitative improvement in corrosion resistance and the film's long-term stability, especially at elevated temperatures, remain to be determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples: one subjected to the anodic oxidation pre-treatment and one untreated. Embed both in identically prepared saline soil molds and expose them at controlled room temperature and elevated temperature conditions. Periodically (e.g., at 14, 28, and 120 days) conduct EIS, weight loss, and polarisation measurements.
measurements: Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to measure charge transfer resistance.
Potentiodynamic polarisation curves to determine corrosion kinetics.
Weight loss measurements for corrosion rate quantification.
SEM imaging to inspect surface morphology and film integrity.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement (e.g., >20% increased charge transfer resistance or reduced weight loss) relative to untreated samples under both temperature regimes, the hypothesis is falsified.

expert_context.question: Earlier studies on stainless, alloy, and boiler steels reported improved hardness, wear resistance, thermal stability, or reduced mass change during aggressive salt exposure at 700–900 °C. However, these findings were specific to individual material systems and emphasized characterization or performance rather than establishing why corrosion protection persists or fails across room- and high-temperature regimes; studies combining HEAs, subsequent annealing, and hot-corrosion assessment were also reported to be minimal. For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain its corrosion-related degradation or retention of protection under these regimes? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to an appropriate reference, the conditions under which the hypothesis should and should not apply, supporting evidence from the earlier studies, and an observation that would falsify it.

final_hypothesis.label: C5

source_paper.title: An electrochemical study of pH influences on corrosion and passivation for a Q235 carbon steel in HNO3-NaNO2, HAc-NaNO2 and HCl-NaNO2 solutions.

final_hypothesis.builds_on: the observation in PMC9076090 linking activation–passivation behavior with grain-boundary dissolution, suggesting that microstructural inhomogeneities influence passivation.
final_hypothesis.what_is_new: It introduces a controlled annealing step to intentionally homogenize the microstructure as a strategy to improve corrosion protection, a variable not explored in the referenced study.

hypothesis.hypothesis: The heterogeneity at the grain boundaries of Q235 steel governs the initiation and propagation of corrosion under both ambient and high-temperature salt exposure. Homogenizing the microstructure via controlled annealing prior to exposure enhances the uniformity and robustness of the passivation layer by reducing preferential attack sites.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: As-received Q235 steel with a heterogeneous microstructure characterized by variable grain boundary compositions and localized inclusions.
hypothesis.intervention: Subject one set of Q235 steel samples to a controlled annealing treatment designed to homogenize the grain size and boundary chemistry without inducing additional phase changes. Compare these annealed samples to as-received, non-annealed specimens during room-temperature and high-temperature salt exposure tests.
hypothesis.conditions: Corrosion tests conducted in ambient electrochemical cells and hot-corrosion tests in salt deposits at 700–900 °C; the hypothesis applies when grain-boundary heterogeneities are significant corrosion initiation sites.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A uniform microstructure with reduced heterogeneity at grain boundaries mitigates localized dissolution, leading to a more uniform and adherent passive film formation.
hypothesis.mechanism: Heterogeneous grain boundaries serve as weak links where corrosion and pitting initiate, as seen from the correlation between passivation transitions and grain boundary dissolution in PMC9076090. Annealing reduces these microstructural disparities, resulting in a passive film that is more continuous, thus improving corrosion resistance both at room temperature and under high-temperature salt stress.
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Annealed Q235 steel specimens are expected to exhibit lower corrosion current densities and reduced mass change during high-temperature salt exposure compared to non-annealed specimens; microscopy should reveal fewer localized corrosion pits along grain boundaries in the annealed samples.
hypothesis.baseline: Non-annealed, as-received Q235 steel tested under the same conditions.
hypothesis.boundary: This mechanism is operative when grain-boundary heterogeneity is the dominant factor. If the corrosion is governed by other factors (e.g., environmental aggressiveness overcoming microstructural effects), the improvement may be minimal.
hypothesis.uncertainty: Quantitative improvements (e.g., percentage reduction in mass loss) are not precisely predicted without further microstructural analysis.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of specimens (annealed and as-received) and subject them to identical electrochemical and hot-corrosion tests. Use microscopy to characterize grain boundaries and mapping of corrosion pit locations. Correlate the microstructural uniformity with corrosion metrics.
measurements: Corrosion current densities (icorr) from polarization tests
Mass loss measurements in high-temperature salt baths
Grain boundary characterization via SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit significant improvements in corrosion resistance (electrochemical stability or mass change) or show similar grain-boundary initiated corrosion sites as the as-received samples, the hypothesis is falsified.

source_paper.title: High-Temperature Corrosion of Ni-Cr-Mo Cladding Layers with Different Si Contents in NaCl-KCl-Na2SO4-K2SO4 Mixed Salt Medium.

top3.builds_on: The concept that structure (e.g., oxide film integrity) controls corrosion performance as seen in the dense Cr-rich oxides in the Ni-Cr-Mo system (PMC9100067::web::019) inspires a microstructural approach for plain steel.
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis suggests altering the substrate microstructure through controlled annealing—as opposed to compositional changes or surface depositions—to indirectly improve the quality of the oxide scale and hence the corrosion protection under hot-corrosion conditions.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Grain Refinement/Coarsening Control via Pre-corrosion Annealing to Modify Oxide Scale Pathways.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: As-received Q235 steel with a typical fine-grained microstructure that may have high grain boundary density facilitating corrosive species penetration.
hypothesis.intervention: Apply a controlled annealing treatment below the austenitization temperature to induce moderate grain coarsening in the near-surface region, thereby reducing the density of grain boundaries.
hypothesis.conditions: The intervention is carried out before any corrosive exposure. It is expected to be effective in high-temperature salt environments (above 700 °C), where grain boundaries in the oxide scale can act as rapid diffusion paths for corrosive species. The mechanism may not significantly affect room-temperature corrosion, where grain boundary diffusion is slower.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: A coarser near-surface microstructure in the steel substrate, which promotes the formation of an oxide scale with fewer grain boundaries and defects.
hypothesis.mechanism: Grain boundaries often serve as fast diffusion paths for oxygen, Cl–, and other aggressive ions. By reducing the grain boundary density through controlled annealing, the resultant oxide scale formed during high-temperature corrosion is expected to be more uniform and less permeable. This barrier effect reduces corrosion rates. A similar idea of controlling microstructural features to influence oxide scale integrity is observed in studies on high-temperature oxide films (e.g., as discussed in materials teaching texts on high-temperature oxidation TXT::wikipedia::Stainless_steel::028).
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Annealed Q235 steel with a coarser near-surface microstructure should exhibit a more adherent and uniform oxide film with fewer defects, resulting in lower weight loss and less pitting under high-temperature salt exposure compared to as-received, fine-grained samples.
hypothesis.baseline: Q235 steel in the as-received, fine-grained condition with a higher density of grain boundaries and, consequently, more defect-prone oxide scales.
hypothesis.boundary: This approach may be limited by potential negative impacts on mechanical properties if grain growth is excessive and may not influence corrosion mechanisms at room temperature where diffusion rates are lower.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The precise extent of grain coarsening required for a measurable improvement is uncertain and would need to be optimized experimentally.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Q235 steel samples: one subjected to controlled annealing designed to coarsen near-surface grains and the other kept in the as-received condition. Expose both sets to identical high-temperature salt environments (700–900 °C) and compare corrosion kinetics by measuring weight loss, oxide scale uniformity (via SEM), and grain boundary mapping (via EBSD).
measurements: Weight loss per unit area
SEM and EBSD analysis of oxide scale and substrate microstructure
Pit density assessment
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed (coarser) samples do not show statistically significant improvements in oxide scale uniformity and reduced corrosion (lower weight loss and pit density) compared to the as-received samples, then the hypothesis is falsified.

top3.label: C1

source_paper.title: Research on the Corrosion Behavior of Q235 Pipeline Steel in an Atmospheric Environment through Experiment.

top3.builds_on: the paper’s detailed description of the transition from intact passivation to localized corrosion linked to film breakdown (PMC9504384::web::009, PMC9504384::web::016)
top3.what_is_new: This hypothesis introduces a pre-passivation cleaning modification aimed at lowering chloride-induced weaknesses in the passivation film—a factor not explicitly isolated in the paper—to test its effect on corrosion retention across different temperature regimes.

hypothesis.hypothesis: Residual chloride contamination in the passivation film is a critical factor that promotes localized corrosion initiation; an enhanced cleaning step before passivation that more effectively removes chloride species will improve long-term corrosion protection even during high-temperature, aggressive salt exposure.
hypothesis.material_initial_state: Q235 steel after standard pickling and passivation treatment that may retain trace chloride compounds from salt contamination or cleaning processes.
hypothesis.intervention: Implement an additional decontamination stage (e.g., an ultrasonic cleaning in deionized water or an acid rinse optimized for chloride removal) prior to passivation.
hypothesis.conditions: Testing under both ambient cyclic salt spray and high-temperature exposure (700–900 °C) where the aggressive salt environment could activate chloride-induced corrosion mechanisms.
hypothesis.structural_mediator: Reduction of residual chloride ions within the passivation film, which in untreated samples serve as nucleation sites for film rupture and subsequent localized corrosion.
hypothesis.mechanism: Chloride ions embedded in or near the passivation film compromise its integrity during thermal cycling, accelerating the degradation to a rapidly growing rust layer. By ensuring a cleaner surface before passivation, the formation of a more uniform and robust protective layer is promoted, thus delaying or mitigating the transition from passivation film to full-blown corrosion (PMC9504384::web::016).
hypothesis.predicted_outcome: Samples undergoing the enhanced cleaning will exhibit reduced localized pitting, slower transition to the second protective layer failure, and overall lower corrosion weight loss compared to conventionally processed samples under identical salt spray tests. Predicted improvements are qualitative given uncertainties in chloride removal efficiency.
hypothesis.baseline: Q235 steel processed by the standard industrial pickling and passivation method without the enhanced cleaning step.
hypothesis.boundary: This approach is expected to work primarily for Q235 steel where chloride retention is a significant issue. Its efficacy may be reduced if chloride contamination originates from the test medium rather than the pre-treatment.
hypothesis.uncertainty: The degree of improvement in corrosion resistance depends on the efficiency of chloride removal and the re-contamination potential during subsequent processing; precise quantification is uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Q235 steel specimens: one following the standard cleaning/passivation and the other including the enhanced decontamination step. Subject both groups to identical cyclic salt spray tests under high-temperature conditions (700–900 °C). Evaluate initiation sites of pitting and overall corrosion progression using weight loss measurements and microscopic surface analysis.
measurements: Corrosion weight loss over time
Microscopic (SEM) analysis of pitting density and distribution
Surface chloride quantification (e.g., via XPS or EDS) prior to exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the enhanced cleaning group shows no statistically significant reduction in localized corrosion or weight loss compared to the control group, the hypothesis is falsified.
